etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English trikke, from Old Northern French trique (related to Old French trichier (“to defraud, act dishonestly, conceal, deceive, cheat”); > modern French tricher), itself possibly from Middle High German trechen (“to launch a shot at, play a trick on”), or one of its derivatives (e.g. Middle High German ūftrechen (“to do something to someone, hurt someone”), vertrechen (“to conceal, get over on someone”), zuotrechen (“to obtain falsely or deceitfully, wangle, finagle”), etc.); yet the Old French verb is equally likely to be derived from Vulgar Latin *triccāre, from Late Latin tricāre, from Latin trīcor, trīcārī (“dodge, search for detours; haggle, quibble”).

The term has been connected to Middle Dutch treck, trec (“draw, line, desire, game move, cord, stratagem, ruse, trick”), from Middle Dutch trekken, trēken (“to pull, place, put, move”), from Old Dutch *trekken, *trekan (“to move, drag”), from Proto-Germanic *trakjaną, *trekaną (“to drag, scrape, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dreg- (“to drag, scrape”). If they are related, trick would be cognate with Low German trekken, Middle High German trecken, trechen, Danish trække, and Old Frisian trekka, Romanian truc and other Romance languages.

Compare track, treachery, trig, and trigger.

definitions.definition: Something designed to fool, outsmart or swindle.
A single element of a magician's (or any variety entertainer's) act; a magic trick.
An entertaining difficult physical action.

quote.citation: 1995, All Aboard for Space: Introducing Space to Youngsters, page 158:
quote.text: Yo-yo tricks involving sleeping the yo-yo (like "walking the dog" and "rocking the baby") cannot be performed in space.

definitions.definition: An effective, clever or quick way of doing something.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “Welcome to the plastisphere”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Plastics are energy-rich substances, which is why many of them burn so readily. Any organism that could unlock and use that energy would do well in the Anthropocene. Terrestrial bacteria and fungi which can manage this trick are already familiar to experts in the field.

definitions.definition: Mischievous or annoying behavior; a prank.
(dated) A particular habit or manner; a peculiarity; a trait.

quote.citation: c. 1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life and Death of King Iohn”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: He hath a trick of Cœur de Lion's face.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene vi]:
quote.text: The trick of that voice I do well remember.

definitions.definition: A knot, braid, or plait of hair.

quote.citation: 1601, Ben Jonson, Poetaster or The Arraignment: […], London:  […]  [R. Bradock] for M[atthew] L[ownes] […], published 1602, →OCLC, (please specify the page), (please specify the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: I cannot tell , but it stirs me more than all your court curls , or your spangles , or your tricks

definitions.definition: (card games) A sequence in which each player plays a card and a winning play is determined.

quote.citation: 1712, Alexander Pope, “Canto III”, in The Rape of the Lock, lines 93–94; republished in The Complete Poetical Works of Alexander Pope, Boston, New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1902, page 94:
quote.text: And now (as oft in some distemper'd state) / On one nice trick depends the gen'ral fate!

definitions.definition: (slang) A sex act, chiefly one performed for payment; an act of prostitution.

quote.citation: 1988, John H. Lindquist, Misdemeanor Crime: Trivial Criminal Pursuit, page 43:
quote.text: Perhaps the most important thing a prostitute learns is how to "manage" the client; how to con him into spending more money than he planned. Learning how to perform tricks takes only a few minutes. Learning how to "hustle" the client takes longer.

quote.citation: 2010, Richard Gill, Paloma Azul, page 139:
quote.text: "How did you get into all this?" "I started doing tricks when I was young and I don't mean the magic circle. I learned about sex from an early age. There was nothing else to do in Pitsea except heavy petting and getting F grades at school."

quote.citation: 2019, Julie S. Draskoczy, Belomor: Criminality and Creativity in Stalin’s Gulag:
quote.text: When he later asked her to strip and perform tricks for him, she refused, and he chased her away. She had similar experiences with other men until she eventually fell into prostitution:  […]

definitions.definition: (slang) A customer or client of a prostitute.

quote.citation: 2011, Iceberg Slim, Pimp: The Story of My Life, page 99:
quote.text: Ten minutes after she got down she broke luck. A white trick in a thirty-seven Buick picked her up. I timed her. She had racehorse speed.

definitions.definition: (slang, vulgar) A term of abuse.
(Western Pennsylvania) A daily period of work, especially in shift-based jobs.

quote.citation: 1885, Order of Railway Conductors and Brakemen, The Conductor and Brakeman, page 496:
quote.text: On third trick from 12 m. to 8 am, we have W. A. White, formerly operator at Wallula, who thus far has given general satisfaction.

quote.citation: 1899, New York (State), Bureau of Statistics, Deptartment of Labor, Annual Report:
quote.text: Woodside Junction—On 8 hour basis, first trick $60, second trick $60, third trick $50.

quote.citation: 1949, Labor arbitration reports, page 738:
quote.text: The Union contends that Fifer was entitled to promotion to the position of Group Leader on the third trick in the Core Room Department.

definitions.definition: (nautical) A sailor's spell of work at the helm, usually two hours long.

quote.citation: 1902, John Masefield, Sea Fever:
quote.text: I must go down to the seas again, to the vagrant gypsy life,To the gull's way and the whale's way, where the wind's like a whetted knife;And all I ask is a merry yarn from a laughing fellow-rover,And quiet sleep and a sweet dream when the long trick's over.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A toy; a trifle; a plaything.

quote.citation: 1599, [anonymous], “When as Thine Eye hath Chose the Dame”, in The Passionate Pilgrime. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  [Thomas Judson] for W[illiam] Iaggard, and are to be sold by W[illiam] Leake, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The vviles and guiles that vvomen vvorke, / Diſſembled vvith an outvvard ſhevv: / The tricks and toyes that in them lurke, / The Cock that treads thẽ [them] ſhall not knovv,  […]

definitions.definition: (heraldry) A representation of arms that is drawn as an outline with labels to indicate colors.

quote.citation: 1892, George Gatfield, Guide to Printed Books and Manuscripts Relating to English and Foreign Heraldry, page 12:
quote.text: Heraldic Collections of various Heralds and others, containing Arms blazoned and in trick, grants of arms, pedigrees, etc.

quote.citation: 2009, Thomas Daniel Tremlett, Hugh Stanford London, Rolls of Arms, Henry III., page 132:
quote.text: The trick  […]  might be meant for a lion passant or for one rampant embelif  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To fool; to cause to believe something untrue; to deceive.
(heraldry) To draw (as contrasted with to blazon, which is to describe in words).

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms, / Black as his purpose, did the night resemble / When he lay couched in the ominous horse, / Hath now this dread and black complexion smear'd / With heraldry more dismal; head to foot / Now is he total gules; horridly trick'd / With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons  […]

quote.citation: 1601, Ben Jonson, Poetaster or The Arraignment: […], London:  […]  [R. Bradock] for M[atthew] L[ownes] […], published 1602, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: They forget that they are in the statutes:  […]  there they are trick'd, they and their pedigrees.

definitions.definition: To dress; to decorate; to adorn fantastically; often followed by up, off, or out.

quote.citation: 1624, Henry Wotton, “The Seate, and the Worke”, in The Elements of Architecture, […], London:  […]  Iohn Bill, →OCLC, I. part, page 38:
quote.text: [T]his Pillar [the "Compounded Order"] is nothing in effect, but a Medlie, or an Amaſſe of all the precedent Ornaments, making a nevv kinde, by ſtealth, and though the moſt richly tricked, yet the pooreſt in this, that he is a borrovver of all his Beautie.An adjective use.

quote.citation: 1693, [John Locke], “(please specify the section number)”, in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Tricking up their children in fine clothes.

quote.citation: 1735, Alexander Pope, Of the Characters of Women:
quote.text: Trick her off in air.

quote.citation: 1825, Thomas Macaulay, An Essay on John Milton:
quote.text: They are simple, but majestic, records of the feelings of the poet; as little tricked out for the public eye as his diary would have been.

definitions.definition: To engage in prostitution or casual sex.

quote.citation: 1977-1980, Lou Sullivan, personal diary, quoted in 2019, Ellis Martin, Zach Ozma (editors), We Both Laughed In Pleasure
quote.text: […]  and suddenly it was Maryellin, he & I in the bed. The guy was tall, lean & hard. Absolutely lovely body. For me, it was like my old tricking days.

quote.citation: 1985 April 20, Betsy Duren, “Women's Studies Conference: Sex and Culture”, in Gay Community News, page 7:
quote.text: Asked whether one possible way for lesbians to increase sexual satisfaction within a relationship would be to "trick" outside it, Pearlman said that this could be a "terrific turn-on" if done right, but that she generally wouldn't recommend it because of the high risk of jealousy and breakups.

definitions.definition: Involving trickery or deception.
Able to perform tricks.
Defective or unreliable.
(chiefly US, slang) Stylish or cool.
